meta.title: Languages through time
meta.note: Positions mark an approximate centre of each language at its first appearance; dates are approximate and, for reconstructed proto-languages, estimates with wide margins.

families.label: Indo-European
families.description: From Iceland to Bengal; the best-studied family, reconstructed back to Proto-Indo-European.

families.label: Afroasiatic
families.description: Egyptian, the Semitic languages (Akkadian, Aramaic, Hebrew, Arabic, Ge’ez, Amharic) and others across North Africa and the Near East.

families.label: Sino-Tibetan
families.description: Chinese, Tibetan and Burmese, among hundreds of others; probably from northern China.

families.label: Uralic
families.description: From the Urals to Finland and Hungary.

families.label: Austronesian
families.description: From Taiwan across the Pacific and Indian Oceans, from Madagascar to Hawai‘i.

families.label: Niger–Congo
families.description: Africa’s largest family, including the Bantu languages and Yoruba.

families.label: Other families & isolates
families.description: Every other family on the map, each named in its panel: Dravidian, Austroasiatic, Tai–Kadai, Mongolic, Tungusic, Kartvelian, the families of the Americas, Australia and New Guinea, isolates such as Basque and Ainu, and creoles.

languages.name: Proto-Indo-European
languages.summary: The reconstructed ancestor of the Indo-European languages. The leading hypothesis places its speakers on the Pontic–Caspian steppe (the Yamnaya horizon); the main alternative is Anatolia several millennia earlier.

languages.name: Hittite
languages.summary: The oldest well-attested Indo-European language, written in cuneiform at Hattusa. Its decipherment by Bedřich Hrozný (1915) revealed consonants (ḫ) where Saussure had predicted lost ‘laryngeal’ sounds.

languages.name: Tocharian
languages.summary: Two related languages (A and B) known from Buddhist manuscripts found in the oases of the Tarim Basin, the easternmost ancient Indo-European languages.

languages.name: Proto-Indo-Iranian
languages.summary: The common ancestor of the Indo-Aryan and Iranian languages, often associated with the Sintashta culture of the southern Urals.

languages.name: Vedic Sanskrit
languages.summary: The language of the Rigveda, composed in the Punjab and transmitted orally with great precision for centuries before it was written down.

languages.name: Classical Sanskrit
languages.summary: The language codified by the grammarian Pāṇini (c. 4th century BCE). It became the pan-Indian language of learning, literature and religion.
languages.afterlife: Classical and liturgical language today, with few native speakers.

languages.name: Prakrits
languages.summary: The vernacular Middle Indo-Aryan languages, including Pali and the language of Ashoka’s inscriptions (3rd century BCE). Most modern Indo-Aryan languages descend from them.

languages.name: Hindi–Urdu
languages.summary: Hindustani, the language of the Delhi region, developed two standard registers: Hindi (Devanagari script, Sanskrit vocabulary) and Urdu (Perso-Arabic script, Persian and Arabic vocabulary).
languages.speakers: ≈ 345 million native speakers of Hindi, plus ≈ 70 million of Urdu

night.note: From Sanskrit rātri; the *nókʷts word was lost.

languages.name: Bengali
languages.summary: The eastern Indo-Aryan language of Bengal; the Charyapada poems (10th–12th centuries) are its earliest literature.

languages.name: Punjabi
languages.summary: One of the few Indo-European languages with lexical tone, which developed when breathy-voiced consonants lost their breathiness (tonogenesis).

languages.name: Romani
languages.summary: An Indo-Aryan language whose speakers left northern India and reached Europe by the 14th century. Loanwords picked up along the way (Persian, Armenian, Greek) trace the route.

languages.name: Old Persian
languages.summary: The language of the Achaemenid royal inscriptions, above all Darius’s trilingual inscription at Behistun (c. 520 BCE).

languages.name: Middle Persian
languages.summary: Pahlavi, the language of the Sasanian Empire and Zoroastrian literature.

languages.name: Persian
languages.summary: New Persian (Farsi, Dari, Tajik) emerged after the Arab conquest, written in Arabic script and full of Arabic loanwords, yet grammatically Iranian. Unlike Egypt or Syria, Persia did not shift to Arabic.

languages.name: Mycenaean Greek
languages.summary: The earliest attested Greek, written in the Linear B syllabary on palace tablets. Michael Ventris deciphered it in 1952.

languages.name: Ancient Greek

places.label: Colonies in southern Italy and Sicily

languages.summary: The language of Homer, Herodotus and Plato, spoken in many dialects (Attic, Ionic, Doric, Aeolic) and carried by colonists around the Mediterranean and Black Sea.

languages.name: Koine Greek
languages.summary: The ‘common’ Greek that spread with Alexander’s conquests, the lingua franca of the eastern Mediterranean and the language of the New Testament.

languages.name: Medieval Greek
languages.summary: The Greek of the Byzantine Empire, centred on Constantinople.

languages.name: Modern Greek
languages.summary: With more than 3,000 years of written records, Greek has one of the longest documented histories of any language.

languages.name: Classical Armenian
languages.summary: Grabar, written in the alphabet that Mesrop Mashtots created around 405 CE.

languages.name: Armenian
languages.summary: A branch of its own within Indo-European, with Eastern and Western standard varieties.

languages.name: Albanian
languages.summary: A branch of its own within Indo-European, first written in a baptismal formula of 1462. It shares Balkan Sprachbund features, such as a postposed article, with unrelated neighbours.

languages.name: Proto-Balto-Slavic
languages.summary: The reconstructed common ancestor of the Baltic and Slavic languages.

languages.name: Old Prussian
languages.summary: A West Baltic language recorded in vocabularies and catechisms. It died out in the early 18th century as its speakers shifted to German.

languages.name: Lithuanian
languages.summary: Famously conservative: it preserves a rich case system and pitch accent that resemble reconstructed Proto-Indo-European.

languages.name: Latvian
languages.summary: The other living Baltic language, with fixed initial stress and a large Low German vocabulary layer.

languages.name: Proto-Slavic
languages.summary: The common Slavic language, which spread rapidly across eastern and central Europe and the Balkans from the 6th century.

languages.name: Old Church Slavonic
languages.summary: The first written Slavic language, created for the mission of Cyril and Methodius (863) and cultivated at Ohrid and Preslav.
languages.afterlife: Survives as Church Slavonic, the liturgical language of Orthodox Slavs.

languages.name: Old East Slavic
languages.summary: The language of Kievan Rus’, known from chronicles and the birch-bark letters of Novgorod.

languages.name: Russian
languages.summary: Moscow’s language spread east with Russian expansion across Siberia to the Pacific.

languages.name: Ukrainian
languages.summary: An East Slavic language that developed its own standard in the 19th century.

languages.name: Polish
languages.summary: A West Slavic language and one of the few Slavic languages to keep the nasal vowels of Proto-Slavic.

languages.name: Czech
languages.summary: A West Slavic language whose spelling reform (attributed to Jan Hus, early 15th century) introduced diacritics such as the háček, later adopted by other languages.

languages.name: Bosnian–Croatian–Montenegrin–Serbian
languages.summary: One South Slavic language with several national standards, written in Latin and Cyrillic scripts.

languages.name: Bulgarian
languages.summary: A South Slavic language that, through Balkan contact, lost its noun cases and gained a definite article placed after the noun (вълкът ‘the wolf’).

languages.name: Proto-Germanic
languages.summary: The ancestor of the Germanic languages, set apart from the rest of Indo-European by Grimm’s and Verner’s Laws and by fixed stress on the first syllable.

languages.name: Gothic
languages.summary: Known mainly from Bishop Wulfila’s 4th-century Bible translation; the only well-attested East Germanic language. A form of it (Crimean Gothic) was still recorded in the 16th century.

languages.name: Old Norse
languages.summary: The language of the Viking Age and the sagas, carried west to the British Isles, Normandy, Iceland and Greenland.

languages.name: Icelandic
languages.summary: Changed so little in its written form that Icelanders can still read the medieval sagas; it famously embarrassed glottochronology’s constant-rate assumption.

languages.name: Swedish
languages.summary: An East Scandinavian language, largely mutually intelligible with Norwegian and (in writing) Danish.

languages.name: Danish
languages.summary: An East Scandinavian language known for extensive consonant weakening (lenition) in speech.

languages.name: Norwegian
languages.summary: A West Scandinavian language with two written standards, Bokmål and Nynorsk, and strong spoken dialect diversity.

languages.name: Old English
languages.summary: Brought to Britain by Angles, Saxons and Jutes from the 5th century. It had four cases, three genders and verb-second word order; Beowulf is its best-known poem.

languages.name: Middle English
languages.summary: The English of Chaucer, transformed by the loss of inflections and by thousands of Norman French loanwords.

languages.name: English

places.label: The Ohio Valley and the Midwest (from the 1790s)

languages.summary: Early Modern and Modern English: the Great Vowel Shift, the rise of do-support, the loss of thou, and global spread with colonisation, trade and, later, technology.
languages.speakers: ≈ 380 million native speakers; far more as a second language

languages.name: Scots
languages.summary: Descended from Northern Middle English; the language of the Scottish court and its poets before the Union of the Crowns in 1603.

languages.name: Old High German
languages.summary: The southern German dialects that underwent the High German consonant shift (p, t, k → pf/ff, ts/ss, ch).

languages.name: Middle High German
languages.summary: The language of the Nibelungenlied and courtly poetry.

languages.name: German
languages.summary: Standard German grew from East Central German varieties, helped by printing and Luther’s Bible translation (1522–1534).

languages.name: Yiddish

places.label: New York and the Americas (from the 1880s)

languages.summary: The language of Ashkenazi Jews: a Germanic base with Hebrew–Aramaic and Slavic components, written in Hebrew script. Its centre moved east, and later across the Atlantic.

languages.name: Old Dutch
languages.summary: Old Low Franconian, sparsely attested; ‘Hebban olla vogala…’ (c. 1100) is its best-known line.

languages.name: Dutch
languages.summary: A West Germanic language that did not undergo the High German consonant shift (maken, not machen).

languages.name: Afrikaans
languages.summary: Developed from the Dutch of the Cape Colony (founded 1652), restructured through contact with Khoekhoe, Malay, Portuguese and other languages; an official language since 1925.

languages.name: Latin
languages.era: c. 600 BCE – 600 CE as a spoken mother tongue
languages.summary: The language of Rome, spread by conquest across the western Mediterranean. As the empire fragmented, spoken Latin drifted into the Romance languages; in Britain and North Africa it did not survive.
languages.afterlife: Remained the written language of scholarship, law and the Church; still liturgical today.

languages.name: Old French
languages.summary: First recorded in the Strasbourg Oaths of 842. After 1066 its Norman variety became the language of England’s ruling class and left thousands of words in English.

languages.name: French

places.label: West and Central Africa (mostly as a second language, from the late 19th century)

languages.summary: Standardised early (the Académie française dates from 1635). French has gone round Jespersen’s Cycle (ne … pas → pas) and is cycling its future tense (chanterai → je vais chanter).
languages.speakers: ≈ 74 million native speakers; many more as a second language

languages.name: Haitian Creole
languages.summary: Formed in the plantation colony of Saint-Domingue from French vocabulary and West African (especially Gbe) grammatical patterns. Many nouns fused with the French article.

night.note: From French la nuit, with the article fused to the noun (reanalysis).

languages.name: Old Spanish
languages.summary: Castilian, from the northern county of Castile, spread south with the Reconquista.

languages.name: Spanish

places.label: Philippines (colonial language; few native speakers today)

languages.summary: Spread across the Americas from 1492; today the world’s second-largest language by native speakers. Its sound history shows lenition (vita → vida) and the b/v merger.

languages.name: Galician-Portuguese
languages.summary: The medieval language of the northwestern Iberian Peninsula and of the cantigas, lyric poetry admired across Iberia.

languages.name: Portuguese
languages.summary: Carried across the Atlantic and Indian Oceans by Portuguese navigators; most of its speakers today are Brazilian.

languages.name: Catalan
languages.summary: A Romance language of Catalonia, Valencia, the Balearic Islands and Andorra, with a rich medieval literature.

languages.name: Italian
languages.summary: Standard Italian is based on the Tuscan of Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio. Italian keeps Latin’s assimilated consonant clusters (octo → otto, noctem → notte).

languages.name: Romanian
languages.summary: The easternmost Romance language, isolated from the others for over a millennium. It keeps some noun cases and shares Balkan features such as the postposed article (lupul ‘the wolf’).

languages.name: Proto-Celtic
languages.summary: The ancestor of the Celtic languages. Whether it arose in central Europe or along the Atlantic coast is debated.

languages.name: Gaulish
languages.summary: The Celtic language of Gaul, known from inscriptions and the Coligny calendar. Its speakers shifted to Latin under Roman rule.

languages.name: Common Brittonic
languages.summary: The Celtic language of Roman Britain, ancestor of Welsh, Cornish and Breton.

languages.name: Welsh
languages.summary: The most widely spoken Celtic language today, with literature going back to the 6th-century poets Aneirin and Taliesin.

languages.name: Cornish
languages.era: from c. 600; traditional use ended in the late 18th century
languages.summary: Lost its last traditional speakers in the late 18th century (Dolly Pentreath, d. 1777, is the traditional symbol) and was revived by learners in the 20th century.

languages.name: Breton
languages.summary: Taken from Britain to Brittany by migrants in the 5th–6th centuries, so its closest relatives are Cornish and Welsh rather than Gaulish.

languages.name: Old Irish
languages.summary: Known from glosses in monastic manuscripts, with a famously complex verb system.

night.note: The old root survives in in-nocht ‘tonight’.

languages.name: Irish
languages.summary: Once spoken across Ireland; the shift to English accelerated after the Famine of the 1840s. Today it is an official language with a small community of daily speakers.

languages.name: Scottish Gaelic
languages.summary: Carried from Ireland to Scotland; emigration took it to Nova Scotia, where a small community still speaks it.

languages.name: Manx
languages.era: from c. 1200; last traditional native speaker died 1974
languages.summary: Its last traditional native speaker, Ned Maddrell, died in 1974. It has since been revived and is taught in schools on the Isle of Man.

languages.name: Egyptian
languages.summary: Attested for more than three millennia in hieroglyphic, hieratic and demotic writing, through Old, Middle and Late Egyptian.

languages.name: Coptic
languages.era: c. 200 – 17th century as a spoken language
languages.summary: The last stage of Egyptian, written in a Greek-based alphabet. It was gradually replaced by Arabic after the 7th-century conquest.
languages.afterlife: Liturgical language of the Coptic Church.

languages.name: Proto-Semitic
languages.summary: The reconstructed ancestor of the Semitic languages. A Bayesian analysis dates it to about 3750 BCE in the Levant.

languages.name: Akkadian
languages.summary: The language of Babylon and Assyria, written in cuneiform borrowed from Sumerian. Aramaic replaced it in speech during the 1st millennium BCE; scribes kept writing it until about 75 CE.

languages.name: Aramaic

places.label: Lingua franca of the Persian Empire

languages.summary: Spread from Syria to become the common language of the Assyrian and Persian empires, displacing Akkadian. Neo-Aramaic varieties survive but are endangered.

languages.name: Biblical Hebrew
languages.era: c. 1000 BCE – 200 CE as a spoken language
languages.summary: The language of the Hebrew Bible. It ceased to be an everyday mother tongue around the 2nd century CE but continued for nearly two millennia in liturgy, scholarship and writing.

languages.name: Modern Hebrew
languages.summary: The only clear case of a language without native speakers becoming a national mother tongue again, through the revival movement associated with Eliezer Ben-Yehuda.

languages.name: Arabic
languages.era: inscriptions from the 4th century; Qur’an 7th century
languages.summary: Spread with the Islamic conquests from Arabia to the Atlantic, replacing Coptic, Aramaic and much of Berber in everyday speech, but not Persian. The written Classical standard coexists with many spoken varieties (diglossia).
languages.speakers: over 300 million native speakers across its varieties

languages.name: Maltese
languages.summary: Descended from Siculo-Arabic, written in the Latin alphabet, and full of Sicilian, Italian and English loanwords: a Semitic language shaped by European contact.

languages.name: Ge’ez
languages.era: c. 4th – 10th century as a spoken language
languages.summary: The language of the kingdom of Aksum, written in its own script.
languages.afterlife: Liturgical language of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

languages.name: Amharic
languages.summary: A sister of Ge’ez rather than its descendant, and Ethiopia’s working language, written in the Ge’ez script.

languages.name: Proto-Uralic
languages.summary: The reconstructed ancestor of the Uralic languages, usually placed near the Ural Mountains or the Volga–Kama region.

languages.name: Hungarian
languages.summary: Carried from the steppes west of the Urals into the Carpathian Basin by the Magyars around 895. Its first connected text is the Funeral Sermon of about 1192.

languages.name: Proto-Finnic
languages.summary: The common ancestor of Finnish, Estonian and their close relatives around the Gulf of Finland.

languages.name: Finnish
languages.summary: First written by Mikael Agricola (ABC book, 1543). Finnish preserves many very old Germanic and Baltic loanwords.

languages.name: Estonian
languages.summary: A close relative of Finnish, heavily influenced by centuries of contact with Low German.

languages.name: Proto-Turkic
languages.summary: The reconstructed ancestor of the Turkic languages, placed in Mongolia and the surrounding steppe. A phylogenetic study dates it to roughly 2,100 years ago.

languages.name: Old Turkic
languages.summary: The language of the 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions in Mongolia, written in a runic-looking script.

languages.name: Turkish
languages.summary: Oghuz Turkic arrived in Anatolia with the Seljuks after 1071, thousands of kilometres from the Turkic homeland. The 1928 alphabet reform replaced Arabic script with Latin.

night.note: The old word tün survives in dün ‘yesterday’.

languages.name: Kazakh
languages.summary: A Kipchak Turkic language of the Central Asian steppe.

languages.name: Proto-Sino-Tibetan
languages.summary: The reconstructed ancestor of Chinese, Tibetan, Burmese and hundreds of other languages. Two 2019 phylogenetic studies place it in northern China about 6,000–7,000 years ago.

languages.name: Old Chinese
languages.summary: First written on the Shang oracle bones at Anyang. Its pronunciation is reconstructed from rhymes, character components and later dialects.

languages.name: Middle Chinese
languages.summary: The language codified in the Qieyun rhyme dictionary (601 CE), ancestral to most modern Chinese varieties and the source of Sino-Japanese, Sino-Korean and Sino-Vietnamese vocabulary.

languages.name: Mandarin Chinese
languages.summary: The northern Chinese varieties, centred on Beijing; standard Mandarin is the most widely spoken first language in the world.

languages.name: Cantonese
languages.summary: A Yue variety that keeps Middle Chinese final stops (-p, -t, -k) and has six or more tones.

languages.name: Old Tibetan
languages.summary: Written from the 7th century in a script derived from Indian Brahmi; its conservative spelling preserves consonant clusters that later dropped out of speech.

languages.name: Burmese
languages.summary: First written in the Myazedi inscription at Bagan (1113).

languages.name: Proto-Austronesian
languages.summary: The ancestor of more than 1,200 languages. Most early branches are found on Taiwan, the most likely homeland.

languages.name: Proto-Malayo-Polynesian
languages.summary: The language of the first Austronesian settlers outside Taiwan, in the northern Philippines.

languages.name: Malay

places.label: Malacca: lingua franca of maritime trade

languages.summary: First written under the Srivijaya empire, Malay became the trade language of the archipelago. Its standard is now the national language of Malaysia and, as Indonesian, of Indonesia.

languages.name: Tagalog
languages.summary: The basis of Filipino, the national language of the Philippines; it contains many Spanish and English loanwords.

languages.name: Malagasy
languages.summary: Spoken in Madagascar but closest to the Barito languages of southeast Borneo, 7,000 km away: evidence of an Austronesian voyage across the Indian Ocean.

languages.name: Proto-Oceanic
languages.summary: Associated with the Lapita culture of the Bismarck Archipelago, from which people first settled the remote Pacific.

languages.name: Proto-Polynesian
languages.summary: Spoken in Tonga and Samoa, where Polynesian culture took shape before the long voyages east.

languages.name: Samoan
languages.summary: One of the larger Polynesian languages.

languages.name: Hawaiian
languages.summary: Brought by voyagers from central East Polynesia. After near-loss in the 20th century, immersion schools have revived it.

languages.name: Māori
languages.summary: New Zealand was among the last major landmasses settled by humans. Māori is now an official language and the focus of revitalisation.

languages.name: Proto-Bantu
languages.summary: From the Cameroon–Nigeria borderlands, Bantu-speaking farmers spread over most of central, eastern and southern Africa in the following millennia.

languages.name: Swahili
languages.summary: A Bantu language of the East African coast, rich in Arabic loanwords from Indian Ocean trade; today a lingua franca for tens of millions.
languages.speakers: tens of millions of speakers, mostly as a second language

languages.name: Zulu
languages.summary: A Nguni Bantu language whose click consonants were borrowed through contact with Khoisan languages.

languages.name: Yoruba
languages.summary: A tonal language of southwestern Nigeria and Benin; carried across the Atlantic by enslaved people, it survives in Cuban and Brazilian religious practice.

languages.name: Proto-Dravidian
languages.summary: The ancestor of Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and some 80 other languages of South Asia.

languages.name: Tamil
languages.summary: One of the world’s oldest continuously used literary languages (Sangam poetry). Dravidian contact is widely credited with giving Indo-Aryan its retroflex consonants.

languages.name: Old Japanese
languages.summary: The language of the Nara period, recorded in Chinese characters used for their sound (man’yōgana).

languages.name: Japanese
languages.summary: Writes with three scripts, and roughly half of the words in a Japanese dictionary are Sino-Japanese, borrowed from Middle Chinese.

languages.name: Korean
languages.era: from the Silla period; Hangul created 1443
languages.summary: The language of the Korean peninsula. King Sejong’s Hangul (1443) is a featural alphabet whose letter shapes reflect how sounds are made.

languages.name: Nahuatl
languages.summary: The language of the Aztec Empire and a lingua franca of early colonial Mexico. English owes it tomato, chocolate and avocado, via Spanish.

languages.name: Quechua

places.label: Lingua franca of the Inca Empire (15th century)

languages.summary: A family of closely related varieties from central Peru, spread through the Andes by the Inca state and later by Spanish missionaries.

languages.name: Classic Maya
languages.summary: The prestige language of Maya hieroglyphic inscriptions, ancestral to the Ch’olan languages still spoken today.

languages.name: Basque
languages.summary: The only surviving language of western Europe that predates the arrival of Indo-European. Its ancestor, Aquitanian, appears in Roman-era personal and divine names.

languages.name: Sumerian
languages.era: c. 3100–1800 BCE as a spoken language
languages.summary: The language of the earliest writing, in Uruk. Akkadian replaced it in speech by about 1800 BCE.
languages.afterlife: Remained a scholarly and religious written language for well over a thousand years.

languages.name: Etruscan
languages.summary: A non-Indo-European language of central Italy, written in an alphabet adapted from Greek. It was replaced by Latin.

languages.name: Tok Pisin
languages.summary: Grew out of a Pacific plantation pidgin. It is now an official language of Papua New Guinea and the first language of a growing number of speakers.

languages.name: Proto-Eskimo
languages.summary: The reconstructed ancestor of the Yupik and Inuit languages, spoken around the Bering Strait. Its Inuit branch later spread across the whole North American Arctic.

languages.name: Inuit (Iñupiaq, Inuktitut, Kalaallisut)
languages.era: spread east from northern Alaska c. 1000–1300

places.label: Greenland (c. 1300), where Norse settlers were already living

languages.summary: Carried by the Thule people from northern Alaska across Arctic Canada to Greenland within two or three centuries, one of the fastest long-distance spreads of any language. The varieties still form a dialect chain from Alaska to Greenland; Kalaallisut (Greenlandic) is Greenland’s official language.

languages.name: Proto-Athabaskan
languages.summary: The ancestor of the Athabaskan (Dene) languages of interior Alaska and northwestern Canada. One southern branch later migrated thousands of kilometres south.

languages.name: Navajo
languages.summary: Navajo and the Apache languages are close relatives of languages spoken 3,000 km to the north in Canada and Alaska: their ancestors migrated south, reaching the Southwest around the 15th century. Navajo is the most widely spoken Indigenous language in the United States, and in the Second World War the Navajo Code Talkers used it for military communications.

languages.name: Proto-Algonquian
languages.summary: Ancestor of a family stretching from the Rockies to the Atlantic, including Cree, Ojibwe, Blackfoot, Cheyenne and the languages of the East Coast. Leonard Bloomfield’s reconstruction of it showed that regular sound correspondences, and so the comparative method, work just as well for languages without written history.

languages.name: Cree
languages.summary: A chain of dialects from the Rockies to Labrador and one of the most widely spoken Indigenous languages of Canada. Many communities write it in syllabics, a script devised by the missionary James Evans around 1840 and soon adopted by Cree readers.

languages.name: Ojibwe
languages.summary: An Algonquian language of the Great Lakes region, spoken in Canada and the United States. English totem comes from Ojibwe doodem ‘clan’.

languages.name: Massachusett (Wampanoag)
languages.era: texts from 1663; silent in the 19th century; revived since 1993
languages.summary: John Eliot’s translation (1663) was the first Bible printed in the Americas, and Native writers left letters, deeds and wills in the language. It stopped being spoken in the 19th century; since 1993 the Wôpanâak Language Reclamation Project has brought it back to life from those documents.

languages.name: Cherokee

places.label: Oklahoma, after the forced removal of 1838–39 (the Trail of Tears)

languages.summary: Sequoyah, who could not read any language, created a syllabary for Cherokee in 1821. Within a few years much of the nation was literate, and the bilingual Cherokee Phoenix newspaper appeared in 1828.

languages.name: Lakota
languages.summary: A Siouan language of the northern Plains, closely related to Dakota. Most first-language speakers are elderly, and immersion schools are working to reverse the decline.

languages.name: Proto-Uto-Aztecan
languages.summary: Ancestor of languages from Idaho to El Salvador, including Shoshone, Comanche, Hopi, O’odham and Nahuatl. Whether its homeland was in the US Southwest or in Mesoamerica is disputed, a question tied to the spread of maize farming.

languages.name: Hopi
languages.era: on the Hopi mesas of Arizona
languages.summary: Spoken in villages on the Hopi mesas. Benjamin Lee Whorf’s claim that Hopi had no words for time became famous in debates about language and thought; Ekkehart Malotki’s Hopi Time (1983) showed that Hopi has a rich vocabulary for it.

languages.name: Comanche
languages.era: on the southern Plains from c. 1700
languages.summary: Comanche split from Shoshone around 1700, when its speakers, newly mounted on horses, moved from the Great Basin onto the southern Plains. Comanche code talkers served in the Second World War.

languages.name: Proto-Mayan
languages.summary: Reconstructed by Terrence Kaufman and others and usually placed in the Cuchumatanes highlands of western Guatemala. About thirty Mayan languages descend from it.

languages.name: Yucatec Maya
languages.era: texts in Latin script from the 16th century
languages.summary: The Mayan language of the Yucatán Peninsula, recorded in the colonial Books of Chilam Balam and still widely spoken.

languages.name: Kʼicheʼ
languages.era: Popol Vuh written down in the mid-16th century
languages.summary: The most widely spoken Mayan language of Guatemala. The Popol Vuh, the Kʼicheʼ book of creation, was written in Latin letters in the mid-16th century.

languages.name: Zapotec
languages.summary: Zapotec writing at Monte Albán and San José Mogote is among the earliest in Mesoamerica. ‘Zapotec’ today is a cluster of dozens of tonal varieties, many of them mutually unintelligible.

languages.name: Taíno
languages.summary: The language of the people Columbus met in 1492. It vanished within a century of conquest, but survives in words borrowed through Spanish: hurricane, canoe, hammock and maize.

languages.name: Jamaican Patois
languages.summary: Formed on Jamaica’s sugar plantations from English and West African languages, notably Akan. Most Jamaicans speak it alongside Standard English, in a continuum that runs from broad creole to the standard.

languages.name: Papiamento
languages.summary: The creole of Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire, with vocabulary mostly from Portuguese and Spanish and later Dutch; whether it began as a Portuguese or a Spanish creole is debated. Unusually for a creole, it is used by every social class and is an official language of Aruba and Curaçao.

languages.name: Proto-Tupí–Guaraní
languages.summary: The ancestor of the Tupí–Guaraní languages, which spread along rivers and coasts over a huge part of South America. The wider Tupian family probably began in the southwestern Amazon.

languages.name: Old Tupi
languages.summary: The Tupinambá language of the Brazilian coast, described by the Jesuit José de Anchieta (1595). As the ‘Língua Geral’ it was the everyday lingua franca of colonial Brazil until the 18th century. English owes it jaguar, piranha, tapioca and toucan.

languages.name: Nheengatu
languages.summary: The ‘Língua Geral Amazônica’, the Amazonian descendant of colonial Tupi. It is still spoken along the Rio Negro, where it became the language of peoples who once spoke other languages, and is co-official in São Gabriel da Cachoeira.

languages.name: Guarani
languages.summary: Co-official with Spanish in Paraguay and spoken by most Paraguayans, Indigenous or not, which is unusual among the Indigenous languages of the Americas. The Jesuit missions (1609–1767) used and printed it.
languages.speakers: spoken by most of Paraguay’s population

languages.name: Aymara
languages.summary: The second great language family of the Andes, long in contact with Quechua and sharing much vocabulary and structure with it. Aymara speakers talk and gesture as if the past lies ahead of them and the future behind.

languages.name: Mapudungun
languages.summary: The language of the Mapuche of Chile and Argentina, who resisted both the Inca and the Spanish; Chile and Argentina conquered their lands only in the 1880s. Its first grammar, by Luis de Valdivia, was printed in Lima in 1606.

languages.name: Igbo
languages.summary: A tonal language of southeastern Nigeria. Chinua Achebe’s novels carried Igbo proverbs and words to readers worldwide.

languages.name: Akan (Twi, Fante)
languages.era: language of the Asante kingdom (from c. 1700)
languages.summary: The most widely spoken language of Ghana and the language of the Asante kingdom. Through the Atlantic slave trade it left its mark on Caribbean creoles: Anansi the spider and day-names such as Kofi and Cudjoe crossed with it.

languages.name: Wolof
languages.summary: The lingua franca of Senegal, spoken as a first or second language by most Senegalese. Urban Wolof mixes freely with French.

languages.name: Fula (Fulfulde, Pulaar)
languages.era: spread east across the Sahel from c. 1000

places.label: Macina, in the inner Niger delta

languages.summary: Carried by Fulani herders across the Sahel from Senegal to Cameroon and Sudan, and now spoken in some twenty countries. Fulani-led states such as the Sokoto Caliphate (1804) spread it further.
languages.speakers: tens of millions of speakers in some twenty countries

languages.name: Manding (Bambara, Mandinka, Dyula)
languages.branch: Mande (its place in Niger–Congo is debated)
languages.era: language of the Mali Empire (from the 13th century)
languages.summary: The language of the Mali Empire founded by Sundiata Keita in the 13th century, and of the griots who keep its epic alive. Bambara is now Mali’s lingua franca and Dyula a trade language of Côte d’Ivoire and Burkina Faso; Solomana Kanté created the N’Ko alphabet for it in 1949.

languages.name: Kikongo
languages.summary: The language of the Kingdom of Kongo, which corresponded with Portugal from the 1480s. A catechism printed in Kikongo in 1624 is the oldest surviving book in any Bantu language.

languages.name: Lingala
languages.era: trade language from the late 19th century
languages.summary: Grew out of Bobangi, a trade language of the middle Congo River, after the colonial state adopted it at its river posts in the 1880s. It is now the language of Kinshasa’s streets, of the army and of Congolese rumba.

languages.name: Luganda
languages.era: language of the Buganda kingdom (from the 14th century)
languages.summary: The language of the Buganda kingdom on the shores of Lake Victoria and a lingua franca of southern Uganda.

languages.name: Kinyarwanda
languages.summary: Spoken by nearly all Rwandans and mutually intelligible with Kirundi, the language of Burundi; together they form one of the largest Bantu languages.

languages.name: Shona
languages.summary: The language of the builders of Great Zimbabwe; the country’s name comes from the Shona dzimba dza mabwe, ‘houses of stone’.

languages.name: Xhosa
languages.summary: A Nguni language with three series of click consonants, borrowed from neighbouring Khoekhoe languages. It was Nelson Mandela’s first language.

languages.name: Hausa
languages.era: Hausa city-states from c. 1000; Ajami texts from the 17th century
languages.summary: The most widely spoken Chadic language and a lingua franca across West Africa. It was written in Arabic script (Ajami) for centuries before Latin script (boko) was adopted under colonial rule.
languages.speakers: tens of millions of first-language speakers and many more second-language speakers

languages.name: Somali
languages.summary: A Cushitic language famous for its oral poetry. After decades of debate between Arabic, Latin and the native Osmanya script, the Latin alphabet was made official in 1972.

languages.name: Oromo
languages.era: expanded north in the 16th century; Latin script (Qubee) from 1991
languages.summary: Ethiopia’s most widely spoken first language. The Oromo migrations of the 16th century carried it far to the north; since 1991 it has been written in a Latin alphabet, Qubee.

languages.name: Berber (Tamazight)
languages.era: Libyco-Berber inscriptions from the 2nd century BCE
languages.summary: Spoken across North Africa before Arabic arrived and still the first language of millions, especially in Morocco and Algeria. The Tuareg kept an ancient alphabet, Tifinagh. Tamazight became an official language of Morocco in 2011 and of Algeria in 2016.

languages.name: Old Nubian
languages.summary: The language of the Christian kingdoms of medieval Nubia, written in an alphabet adapted from Coptic with extra letters taken from Meroitic.

languages.name: Nobiin
languages.summary: The descendant of Old Nubian, spoken along the Nile in southern Egypt and northern Sudan. Lake Nasser, created by the Aswan High Dam in the 1960s, flooded much of its homeland and displaced its speakers.

languages.name: Kanuri
languages.era: language of the Kanem–Bornu empire (9th–19th century)

places.label: Bornu, west of Lake Chad (from the 1380s)

languages.summary: The language of the Kanem–Bornu empire, which lasted about a thousand years around Lake Chad. Its ruling dynasty moved from Kanem, northeast of the lake, to Bornu in the late 14th century.

languages.name: Dholuo
languages.summary: The language of the Luo of Kenya and Tanzania, whose ancestors migrated south from what is now South Sudan in the 15th and 16th centuries.

languages.name: Maasai
languages.summary: The language of Maasai herders in Kenya and Tanzania: a tonal Nilotic language whose basic word order puts the verb first.

languages.name: Khoekhoe (Nama)
languages.summary: The most widely spoken of the non-Bantu click languages of southern Africa, used in Namibia (Nama and Damara) and South Africa. Neighbouring Bantu languages such as Xhosa and Zulu borrowed their clicks from Khoekhoe and related languages.

languages.name: Taa (ǃXóõ)
languages.summary: A language of the Kalahari with one of the largest sound inventories ever recorded, often counted at over 100 consonants, most of them clicks. It has only a few thousand speakers.

languages.name: Nigerian Pidgin
languages.summary: Grew from a coastal trade pidgin into a lingua franca for tens of millions of Nigerians and a first language for millions, especially around Warri and Port Harcourt. The BBC has broadcast in it since 2017.

languages.name: Proto-Pama–Nyungan
languages.summary: The ancestor of most Aboriginal Australian languages, which together cover about seven-eighths of the continent. A phylogenetic study places it in the Gulf Plains of northern Queensland about 6,000 years ago, spreading across a continent people had already lived in for tens of thousands of years.

languages.name: Guugu Yimidhirr
languages.era: word list recorded by Cook’s expedition, 1770
languages.summary: When James Cook’s ship was repaired at the Endeavour River in 1770, his crew wrote down gangurru, which entered English as kangaroo. The language is also known for describing space with compass directions (‘the cup is north of the plate’) rather than left and right.

languages.name: Warlpiri
languages.summary: A desert language with a few thousand speakers, one of the strongest Aboriginal languages today. Warlpiri also has a sign language, used especially during mourning, and young people have created a new mixed language, Light Warlpiri, from Warlpiri, Kriol and English.

languages.name: Pitjantjatjara
languages.summary: A variety of the Western Desert language, spoken around Uluṟu; the Western Desert dialect chain covers a vast part of central and western Australia.

languages.name: Dharug (Sydney language)
languages.summary: The language of the Sydney region, where the British landed in 1788. Within a few decades disease and dispossession had devastated its speakers, but not before English borrowed dingo, wombat, koala, waratah and boomerang from it.

languages.name: Kriol
languages.summary: An English-based creole that took shape at the Roper River mission, founded in 1908, and spread across northern Australia. With some 20,000 speakers it is now one of the largest languages of Aboriginal Australia.

languages.name: Proto-Trans–New Guinea
languages.summary: Ancestor of the largest family of New Guinea, with several hundred languages. Its spread may be linked to early farming in the highlands, one of the world’s independent centres of plant domestication.

languages.name: Enga
languages.summary: One of the largest Papuan languages, spoken in the densely populated highlands. Papua New Guinea has more than 800 languages, the greatest linguistic diversity of any country.

languages.name: Fijian
languages.summary: Fiji was settled by Lapita voyagers around 1000 BCE; Fijian and the Polynesian languages descend from closely related Central Pacific dialects.

languages.name: Tongan
languages.summary: The language of the Kingdom of Tonga, often described as the only Pacific island state never formally colonised.

languages.name: Tahitian
languages.summary: The Society Islands were among the first parts of East Polynesia to be settled, around 1000 CE. From there voyagers reached Hawai‘i, Rapa Nui and New Zealand within a few centuries.

languages.name: Rapa Nui
languages.summary: The language of Easter Island, the most remote inhabited place reached by Polynesian voyagers. The rongorongo script found there has never been deciphered.

languages.name: Chamorro
languages.summary: Guam and the Marianas were reached about 3,500 years ago, apparently directly from the Philippines across some 2,000 km of open sea, one of the longest ocean crossings made by that time. Three centuries of Spanish rule left Chamorro full of Spanish loanwords.

languages.name: Formosan languages (Amis, Atayal, Paiwan…)
languages.era: on Taiwan since the Austronesian beginnings
languages.summary: The Indigenous languages of Taiwan. They make up several of the oldest branches of Austronesian, while all the languages outside Taiwan belong to a single branch, Malayo-Polynesian; this is the main evidence that the family began on Taiwan. Many are now endangered.

languages.name: Old Javanese (Kawi)
languages.summary: The literary language of Java’s Hindu–Buddhist kingdoms, first dated in an inscription of 804; it absorbed a large Sanskrit vocabulary.

languages.name: Javanese
languages.summary: The Austronesian language with the most native speakers. Its speech levels require different words depending on whom you address: ‘eat’ is mangan between equals but dhahar when speaking of a respected person.

languages.name: Cebuano
languages.summary: The second most widely spoken native language of the Philippines, centred on Cebu, where Magellan landed in 1521.

languages.name: Cham
languages.era: Đông Yên Châu inscription, c. 4th century
languages.summary: Carried from Borneo to the coast of Vietnam, where the Đông Yên Châu inscription (c. 4th century) is the oldest known text in any Austronesian language. Centuries beside Mon–Khmer languages gave Cham mainland traits, including tones in some dialects.

languages.name: Proto-Austroasiatic
languages.summary: Ancestor of Vietnamese, Khmer, Mon, the Munda languages of India and well over a hundred others. Its homeland, perhaps in the middle Mekong region, and its possible link to the spread of rice farming are debated.

languages.name: Mon
languages.summary: The language of the Dvaravati kingdoms of central Thailand and later of Lower Burma. Mon culture and writing strongly influenced the Burmese; Mon is still spoken in Myanmar today.

languages.name: Old Khmer
languages.summary: The language of the inscriptions of pre-Angkorian and Angkorian Cambodia, the earliest dated 611 CE. Like Old Javanese and Mon, it absorbed a large Sanskrit vocabulary.

languages.name: Khmer
languages.summary: Cambodia’s national language. Unlike its neighbours Thai, Lao and Vietnamese it has no tones, but it has one of the largest vowel inventories of any language.

languages.name: Vietnamese
languages.era: from the 10th century; Latin-based alphabet (quốc ngữ) from the 17th
languages.summary: Austroasiatic in origin but shaped by a thousand years of Chinese rule: much of its vocabulary is Sino-Vietnamese. Its tones arose from lost final consonants, as Haudricourt showed in 1954. The Latin-based quốc ngữ, developed by missionaries in the 17th century, replaced Chinese characters and chữ Nôm in the 20th.

languages.name: Santali
languages.summary: The largest Munda language, spoken in eastern India, Bangladesh and Nepal; the Munda branch shows how far west Austroasiatic once reached. Raghunath Murmu created the Ol Chiki alphabet for Santali in 1925.

languages.name: Proto-Tai
languages.summary: The ancestor of Thai, Lao, Shan, Zhuang and related languages. Southwestern Tai speakers spread from what is now Guangxi and northern Vietnam into mainland Southeast Asia around the 8th–10th centuries.

languages.name: Thai
languages.summary: Tai speakers founded Sukhothai in the 13th century; a script adapted from Khmer appears on the Ram Khamhaeng inscription traditionally dated 1283, though its authenticity is debated. Thai has five tones and large layers of Khmer, Sanskrit and Pali vocabulary.

languages.name: Lao
languages.summary: Closely related to Thai, and largely mutually intelligible with it. Millions more speak Lao varieties in northeastern Thailand (Isan) than in Laos itself.

languages.name: Zhuang
languages.summary: The language of China’s largest ethnic minority, in Guangxi, long written in Sawndip, a script built from Chinese characters.

languages.name: Ahom
languages.summary: Tai conquerors founded the Ahom kingdom in Assam in 1228. Their language survived in court chronicles (buranjis), but its speakers gradually shifted to Assamese, an Indo-Aryan language.

languages.name: Hmong
languages.era: moved south into Laos and Vietnam in the 18th–19th centuries
languages.summary: Hmong speakers moved south from Guizhou into the mountains of Laos, Vietnam and Thailand in the 18th and 19th centuries. After the Vietnam War many became refugees, so there are now large Hmong communities in Minnesota, California and France. The Romanized Popular Alphabet (1953) marks its tones with final letters.

languages.name: Hokkien (Southern Min)
languages.summary: A Southern Min variety from Fujian. Min split off before Middle Chinese, so it keeps some distinctions older than other Chinese varieties. Emigrants carried it to Taiwan and across Southeast Asia, and English tea comes, via Dutch, from Hokkien tê.

languages.name: Tangut
languages.summary: The language of the Western Xia empire, written in a script of some 6,000 complex characters created in 1036. The Mongols destroyed the empire in 1227 and the language died out within a few centuries; modern scholars have deciphered much of it.

languages.name: Middle Mongol
languages.summary: The language of Genghis Khan’s empire and of the Secret History of the Mongols (13th century). The empire stretched from Korea to Hungary, but Mongolian took root only in Mongolia itself; in the west, the Golden Horde shifted to Turkic.

languages.name: Mongolian
languages.summary: Khalkha Mongolian, the national language of Mongolia. It was written in the vertical Mongol script until 1941–46, when Cyrillic replaced it; Inner Mongolia, in China, still uses the old script.

languages.name: Kalmyk
languages.era: on the lower Volga from c. 1630
languages.summary: Oirat Mongols migrated from Dzungaria to the lower Volga around 1630, making Kalmykia the only Mongolic-speaking region of Europe. Most of them tried to return east in 1771; those who stayed were deported to Siberia in 1943.

languages.name: Jurchen
languages.summary: The language of the Jin dynasty (1115–1234), which ruled northern China; its large script was created in 1119.

languages.name: Manchu

places.label: Court language of the Qing dynasty in Beijing (1644–1912)

languages.summary: The Manchu script, adapted from Mongolian in 1599, became an official script of the Qing empire that ruled China from 1644 to 1912. Manchu speakers later shifted to Chinese and only a handful of elderly speakers remain; the closely related Xibe, carried to Xinjiang by a garrison in 1764, is still spoken.

languages.name: Uzbek
languages.summary: Heir to Chagatai, the Turkic literary language of Timurid Central Asia and of the poet Ali-Shir Nava’i. Persian has deeply influenced it, and its alphabet has changed from Arabic to Latin (late 1920s), to Cyrillic (1940) and back to Latin (1993).

languages.name: Uyghur
languages.summary: Spoken in Xinjiang. Its literary ancestor, Karakhanid Turkic, produced Mahmud al-Kashgari’s dictionary of the Turkic languages (1070s), an early work of comparative linguistics.

languages.name: Sakha (Yakut)
languages.era: on the middle Lena from c. 13th–15th century
languages.summary: The northernmost Turkic language. Its speakers moved north from the Lake Baikal region to the middle Lena between the 13th and 15th centuries, taking up reindeer herding and words from Evenki and Mongolic neighbours.

languages.name: Chuvash
languages.summary: The only surviving Oghur (‘r-Turkic’) language, descended from the speech of the Volga Bulgars. Where other Turkic languages have z, Chuvash has r: Turkish dokuz ‘nine’, Chuvash tăxăr.

languages.name: Azerbaijani
languages.summary: An Oghuz Turkic language very close to Turkish, spoken in Azerbaijan and by a large population in northwestern Iran.

languages.name: Northern Sámi
languages.summary: The largest Sámi language, spoken in northern Norway, Sweden and Finland. Its grammar is built around consonant gradation, and it has a rich vocabulary for snow and reindeer herding.

languages.name: Khanty
languages.era: along the Ob in western Siberia
languages.summary: With Mansi, the closest relative of Hungarian, spoken along the Ob in western Siberia: evidence of where the Hungarians’ ancestors came from. Both are endangered.

languages.name: Mansi
languages.summary: Hungarian’s other close relative, spoken by a few hundred people east of the northern Urals.

languages.name: Nenets
languages.summary: A language of reindeer herders across the tundra from the White Sea to the Yenisei. Samoyedic is one of the two main branches of Uralic.

languages.name: Ket
languages.summary: The last surviving Yeniseian language, spoken by a few dozen people on the Yenisei in central Siberia. Edward Vajda has proposed a relationship with the Na-Dene languages of North America, including Navajo, which would link families on both sides of the Bering Strait; the proposal is debated.

languages.name: Chukchi
languages.summary: The language of reindeer herders and sea-mammal hunters in Russia’s far northeast, known for incorporation (packing nouns into verbs to build very long words) and for differences between women’s and men’s pronunciation.

languages.name: Ainu
languages.summary: The language of the Ainu of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, unrelated to Japanese. Assimilation policies after 1869 brought it close to extinction; Japan recognised the Ainu as an Indigenous people in 2019.

languages.name: Georgian
languages.summary: The largest Kartvelian language, written in its own alphabet since at least the 5th century. Georgian is known for long consonant clusters, as in gvprtskvni ‘you peel us’.

languages.name: Chechen
languages.summary: The largest Northeast Caucasian language. The North Caucasus is one of the most linguistically diverse mountain regions on Earth: Daghestan alone has some thirty languages.

languages.name: Ubykh
languages.summary: Famous for having about 80 consonants and only two or three vowels. After the Russian conquest of the Caucasus in 1864 its speakers were expelled to the Ottoman Empire, where they shifted to Turkish; the last fluent speaker, Tevfik Esenç, died in 1992.

languages.name: Telugu
languages.summary: The most widely spoken Dravidian language, with literature from the 11th century (Nannaya’s Mahabharata). Like the other literary Dravidian languages, it absorbed a great deal of Sanskrit vocabulary.

languages.name: Kannada
languages.summary: A South Dravidian language of Karnataka; the Halmidi inscription (c. 450 CE) is its earliest known text.

languages.name: Malayalam
languages.summary: Grew out of the western coastal dialects of Tamil and became a separate language between about the 9th and 13th centuries, with heavy Sanskrit influence (the mixed literary style called Manipravalam).

languages.name: Brahui
languages.summary: A Dravidian language spoken in Balochistan, Pakistan, more than 1,500 km from the other Dravidian languages and heavily influenced by Balochi. Whether it is a relic of an older Dravidian presence or the result of a later migration is debated.

languages.name: Sinhala
languages.era: Brahmi inscriptions from the 3rd century BCE
languages.summary: Brought to Sri Lanka by Indo-Aryan settlers from northern India. Separated from its relatives by the sea, it developed distinctive features and absorbed Tamil influence.
